name: Churches and Faith Organisations
blurb: Sermon prep, administration, and pastoral limits across hundreds of thousands of congregations, from Barna research and faith-tech platforms to Notre Dame ethics work.

points.desc: Census BTOS covers religious and civic organisations within its service-sector series; no better official measure exists yet, and this page says less rather than guessing.
points.name: Adoption is measured, not guessed

points.desc: The research firm's State of the Church work quantitatively tracks AI adoption, perception, and use among US congregations and ministry leaders - the closest thing to sector-wide survey data.
points.name: Barna Group runs the national studies

points.desc: Used by thousands of US churches, Gloo surveys faith leaders and builds AI tooling for ministry - a primary source for what deployment actually looks like in congregations.
points.name: Gloo is the sector's tech platform

points.desc: The interfaith nonprofit network brings scholars, technologists, and clergy together on the ethical deployment of AI in religious contexts.
points.name: AI and Faith convenes the ethics work

points.desc: The university's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds and tracks research on AI's impact on faith and religious life.
points.name: Notre Dame studies AI and human formation

points.desc: The Hartford Institute for Religion Research regularly surveys congregational trends and digital adoption across American places of worship.
points.name: Hartford surveys congregational technology

points.desc: Pew Research Center's Religion & Public Life work periodically measures how the public and clergy view technology and AI in religious spaces.
points.name: Pew measures public and clergy attitudes

summary: No single body tracks AI adoption across America's hundreds of thousands of congregations - coverage comes from research firms, faith-tech platforms, and academic institutes, and this page names them rather than pretending a census exists. Sermon research, translation, accessibility, and administration are the working uses; every tradition is writing its own guidance.

analysis.body:
AI adoption in churches and faith organisations stands at 13.7% according to the Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey, up from 12.6% in the prior period, placing religious organizations within the broader "Other services" category. This measured adoption reflects early-stage deployment across the country's hundreds of thousands of congregations, though the sources do not specify which types of AI tools or workflows dominate current use in parishes and ministries.

The sector's technology infrastructure centers on purpose-built platforms designed for faith organizations. Gloo, which operates as the primary AI platform for missional leaders, delivers what it describes as values-aligned AI models, developer tools, and benchmarks specifically for faith-based organizations. Gloo's approach addresses a sector-specific concern: its framework measures AI alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing, and it enables organizations to unify siloed data and content to support ministry workflows, knowledge graphs, and mission-specific agents. This emphasis on values alignment reflects a foundational tension in the sector between adopting technology efficiently and maintaining theological and ethical coherence.

Research infrastructure in the sector is substantial but fragmented. Barna Group, a Christian research organization, provides quantitative data on trends affecting faith and ministry through reports like The State of Pastors, tracking how religious leaders navigate AI adoption and cultural change. The Hartford Institute for Religion Research has a 45-year history of surveying congregational life and technology adoption. Pew Research Center's Religion and Public Life division measures public and clergy attitudes toward technology. These organizations collectively track adoption and perception but the sources provided do not disclose specific findings on ROI, deployment costs, or measured outcomes from AI use in congregations.

The ethical and philosophical dimensions of AI adoption in faith contexts receive organized attention. AI and Faith, a pluralist interfaith nonprofit, works to inject what it describes as humility and historicity into AI development by bringing world religions' time-tested values into the ethical AI conversation. The University of Notre Dame's Institute for Ethics and the Common Good funds interdisciplinary research on AI's impact on human formation and religious life, with particular attention to job displacement, worker well-being, and how AI development affects what it means to be human. This scholarship-to-practice pipeline suggests the sector views AI adoption as inseparable from questions of human dignity and spiritual purpose.

A reader considering AI deployment in a faith organization should recognize that adoption remains nascent, that the sector has developed specialized vendor infrastructure designed for values alignment rather than generic commercial AI, and that organized scholarship and ethics networks are active in shaping deployment conversations. The sources do not provide evidence on implementation timelines, cost structures, risk assessments specific to religious contexts, or measured returns from existing deployments. The sector's engagement with the technology appears driven as much by theological and philosophical inquiry as by operational efficiency, suggesting that decisions to adopt should weigh both capability and alignment with organizational values and mission.

https://ethics.nd.edu/.brief: The Notre Dame Institute for Ethics and the Common Good, directed by Meghan Sullivan, conducts interdisciplinary research on artificial intelligence and technology ethics through engagement with industry stakeholders. Sullivan, a Catholic philosopher who meets with AI leaders, reports that many workers in the field discuss job displacement "very flippantly," with some viewing AI's efficiency as an opportunity to shift focus toward family and personal pursuits. Lily Abadal, associated with Catholic school consulting and a faculty fellow on Notre Dame's DELTA project examining human formation in the AI era, notes that awareness of AI's implications has been developing.

https://www.gloo.us/ai.brief: Gloo AI offers faith-based and missional organizations a suite of trusted, values-aligned models, developer tools, and benchmarks to help build AI that reflects their values. The platform provides an API-first system for inference, retrieval-augmented generation, and assistant workflows, along with a connected infrastructure of production tools, trusted content, and models. Gloo AI reports the first comprehensive evaluation framework that measures AI alignment across seven research-backed dimensions of human flourishing. It also supplies knowledge-graph integration, secure infrastructure, and specialized agents that coordinate workflows and power mission-specific solutions, with expert teams designing custom models and infrastructure for missional organizations.

https://aiandfaith.org/.brief: AI and Faith is an organization that brings religious and faith-based perspectives to discussions about artificial intelligence ethics. The group argues that emerging AI issues—including control, privacy, bias, discrimination, and questions about human identity—are fundamentally moral questions, and that the world's religious traditions contain "ancient wisdom" relevant to how AI should be developed and used. The organization works to connect theologians, tech creators, researchers, and ethicists to integrate faith-based values into conversations about AI's ethical implications, aiming to introduce "humility and historicity into an industry that has often rejected them both."
